Pregnancy

Facial swelling in pregnancy: comfort measures and warning signs

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Some gradual swelling is common during pregnancy, particularly in the feet and ankles. New or increasing facial swelling should be discussed with your maternity team. Sudden swelling or swelling with headache, vision changes or other symptoms needs prompt attention before trying home remedies.

Facial swelling deserves a careful check

Pregnancy changes the amount and distribution of fluid in the body. Gradually swollen ankles or feet are common, especially later in the day and later in pregnancy. New swelling of the face is a different reason to pay attention: do not assume it is ordinary fluid retention simply because you are pregnant.

Contact your maternity team promptly about new or increasing facial swelling, particularly around the eyes or when the hands also swell. A sudden increase, headache, changes in vision, pain below the ribs, vomiting or feeling very unwell needs immediate maternity assessment. You do not need all these symptoms before asking for help.

Facial swelling is not an inevitable change that everyone should expect from the first weeks onward. Its cause cannot be established from a photograph, the size of your bump or another person’s experience. Once a clinician has assessed it, you can discuss suitable comfort measures and what changes should prompt another call.

Why fluid collects during pregnancy

The body retains more fluid during pregnancy, and the growing uterus can make it harder for blood to return from the legs. Gravity, long periods of standing and hot weather can make ankle and foot swelling more noticeable. These mechanisms help explain gradual dependent swelling; they do not prove that swelling in every body area is harmless.

Fluid retention does not mean that drinking water has simply raised the sodium concentration of your blood. Salt and water balance is regulated through several body systems, and swelling is not a home test of sodium levels. Restricting fluids or trying to “flush out” swelling with excessive water can be unhelpful and may be unsafe.

Tell the clinician when the change began, whether it affects one or both sides, how quickly it progressed and whether other symptoms are present. Mention new medicines, allergies or a painful area as well. Facial swelling can have causes beyond pregnancy-related fluid retention, so the location and associated symptoms matter.

Pre-eclampsia and the symptoms to act on

Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy complication involving high blood pressure and signs of organ involvement. It usually develops after 20 weeks and can also appear after birth. Swelling alone does not diagnose it, and some people have no obvious symptoms; routine blood-pressure and urine checks are important even when you feel well.

Seek immediate assessment for sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, especially with a persistent or severe headache, blurred vision or flashing lights, pain high in the abdomen or under the ribs, vomiting, or feeling very unwell. New breathlessness is also concerning. Do not wait to see whether drinking water, sleeping or reducing salt makes these symptoms go away.

A home blood-pressure reading can be useful information if you have been asked to monitor, but one normal reading should not override concerning symptoms. Tell the team that you are pregnant or recently gave birth and describe the change clearly. If you cannot reach the usual maternity service promptly, use urgent care or emergency services as appropriate to the symptoms.

Get emergency help for airway symptoms

Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, fainting or collapse may indicate a severe allergic reaction or another emergency. Call your local emergency number immediately. Do not treat this as ordinary pregnancy puffiness or wait for a routine maternity appointment.

If you have a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector for anaphylaxis, use it as instructed and tell the dispatcher. Follow the emergency team’s advice about positioning and further treatment. The need for urgent care is not reduced because the swelling started after a familiar food or medicine.

Severe breathlessness, chest pain, confusion or a seizure also requires emergency help. Different causes can produce overlapping symptoms, and you do not have to decide whether the problem is an allergy, pre-eclampsia or something else before calling.

Rest, movement and position after assessment

If your clinician considers the swelling benign, breaks from prolonged standing or sitting may help comfort. For swollen legs or feet, resting with the feet supported, moving the ankles and taking gentle walks can improve how they feel. These are measures for dependent swelling, not established treatments for unexplained facial swelling.

Avoid staying motionless for long periods just to reduce swelling. Change position regularly and choose activity that is comfortable and appropriate for your pregnancy. If an activity brings on dizziness, pain, fluid leakage, bleeding or other concerning symptoms, stop and seek advice rather than pushing through.

Side-lying with pillows can make rest more comfortable. From 28 weeks, NHS advice is to go to sleep on your side, either left or right. You do not need to remain only on the left all night, and leg elevation or side sleeping should not be presented as a way to prevent or treat pre-eclampsia.

Water, salt and potassium are not a swelling cure

Drink regularly according to thirst, weather, activity and any individualized advice from your care team. Do not deliberately dehydrate yourself to make swelling look smaller, and do not force large volumes of water in an attempt to flush sodium out. If you have a heart, kidney or other condition affecting fluid advice, follow the plan made for you.

A balanced diet can include fruits, vegetables and ordinary sources of potassium, such as bananas or avocado. These foods are not a treatment for facial swelling or high blood pressure in pregnancy. Potassium supplements and salt substitutes can be unsuitable in some medical conditions or with some medicines, so do not start them for swelling without advice.

Choosing fewer very salty processed foods may fit an overall balanced diet, but a strict salt restriction is not recommended solely to prevent pre-eclampsia. Avoid turning chips, takeaway food or a particular meal into an explanation for new facial swelling that needs assessment. Nutrition supports health; it does not replace a blood-pressure check or maternity review.

Heat, swimming and other comfort measures

Heat can make swelling feel worse. Resting in a cooler environment, wearing comfortable clothing and footwear, and avoiding long periods standing in the heat may help ordinary pregnancy discomfort. These choices should support comfort without delaying care for a sudden change.

Gentle swimming may feel comfortable if your maternity clinician considers it appropriate, because the water supports your body. It should not be advertised as a proven way to reduce facial swelling or treat a pregnancy blood-pressure disorder. Check activity advice if you have bleeding, leaking fluid or other complications.

Do not take water tablets, herbal diuretics or products marketed for detoxing or fluid removal unless specifically prescribed or approved for your circumstances. The aim is not to force fluid loss at home. If assessed swelling persists, becomes painful or changes pattern, ask for a review instead of adding more home treatments.

What the assessment may involve

The team may check blood pressure, urine and symptoms, examine the swelling and review your pregnancy history. Blood tests or checks of the baby may be needed if pre-eclampsia or another problem is suspected. Not everyone needs the same investigations; the findings determine the next step.

A dent that remains briefly after pressing swollen skin, called pitting, does not by itself confirm a dangerous cause or rule one out. Nor does improvement overnight guarantee safety. Marked morning swelling or a change that persists is worth mentioning, but no home pattern replaces clinical assessment.

If pre-eclampsia is diagnosed, care can include closer monitoring, blood-pressure treatment and decisions about the safest timing of birth. Severe disease may need hospital care and additional medicines. The plan depends on your condition and the baby’s, not on how much facial puffiness is visible. Ask what symptoms and readings should trigger an immediate call.

Keep watching after the baby is born

Fluid changes can continue during recovery after birth, but pre-eclampsia can also first appear in the postpartum period, including in someone whose blood pressure was normal during pregnancy. New face or hand swelling with headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, vomiting or breathlessness still needs urgent assessment.

Keep the maternity discharge contact details and tell any clinician how recently you gave birth. If you were prescribed blood-pressure medicine or follow-up checks, continue according to the plan rather than stopping when swelling improves. Appearance alone cannot show whether blood pressure or organ function has returned to normal.

You cannot always prevent pre-eclampsia, and developing it is not evidence that you ate the wrong food or failed to rest enough. Attend monitoring and discuss any prescribed prevention plan with your clinician. For day-to-day comfort, use the measures that fit your assessed situation while keeping a clear route back to care if symptoms change.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ordinary lower-limb fluid retention does not establish that new facial swelling is harmless.

Diet, water, exercise and sleep position are comfort considerations, not treatments for suspected pre-eclampsia.

How BeMama can help

Note when swelling began and any accompanying symptoms, then contact the maternity team. After assessment, agree on comfortable activity and the signs that should bring you back for review.

When to seek help

Sudden face/hand swelling with headache, visual changes, upper abdominal pain, vomiting or feeling very unwell needs immediate maternity assessment. Lip/tongue/throat swelling with breathing or swallowing difficulty, collapse or seizures requires emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • New facial swelling should not automatically be labeled normal pregnancy edema.
  • Pre-eclampsia can occur during pregnancy or after birth.
  • Do not use pitting, morning timing or one blood-pressure reading as a complete safety test.
  • After assessment, rest, gentle movement and avoiding heat may help comfort.
  • Avoid dehydration, forced water intake and unprescribed diuretics or potassium supplements.

Frequently asked questions

Is facial swelling normal from the first weeks of pregnancy?

It is not an inevitable change to assume is normal. Discuss new or increasing facial swelling with your maternity team, and seek immediate assessment for a sudden change or accompanying warning symptoms.

Does swelling mean I have pre-eclampsia?

Not by itself. Diagnosis requires clinical assessment, including blood pressure and other findings. Swelling can have several causes.

Should I wait overnight to see whether the swelling improves?

Not when swelling is sudden or accompanied by headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain or feeling unwell. Seek immediate advice; improvement with rest would not establish the cause.

Can drinking lots of water flush the swelling away?

No reliable treatment works that way. Drink regularly and follow individual fluid advice; avoid both deliberate dehydration and forced excessive intake.

Will bananas or avocado treat the swelling?

They can be ordinary parts of a balanced diet, but they are not treatments for facial swelling or pre-eclampsia. Do not add potassium supplements for this purpose without advice.

Do I need a strict low-salt diet to prevent pre-eclampsia?

No. Salt restriction is not recommended solely for that purpose. Follow balanced eating and any individualized medical advice.

Must I sleep only on my left side?

No. NHS advice from 28 weeks is to go to sleep on either side. A comfortable position does not replace assessment of concerning swelling.

Does pitting prove the swelling is dangerous?

No. A dent in swollen skin is one observation, not a diagnosis. Symptoms, examination and appropriate tests determine the cause.

Can pre-eclampsia start after birth?

Yes, including when blood pressure was normal during pregnancy. New swelling with headache, vision changes, pain or breathlessness still needs urgent care.

What if my lips or tongue swell and breathing becomes difficult?

Call your local emergency number immediately. If you have a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector, use it as instructed and follow emergency advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
